```{r}
library(tidyverse)
set.seed(1000)
chep<-readRDS(here::here("Data", "chep_subset.rds"))|>
  slice_sample(n=1000)
model1<-glm(
  REPVOTE  ~ HARDSHIP_INDEX ,
  family = binomial,
  data = chep)

model2<-glm(
  REPVOTE  ~ HARDSHIP_INDEX + VOTE24_CHOICE ,
  family = binomial,
  data = chep)


saveRDS(chep, file=here::here("Data", "chep1000.rds"))
```


## Effects on the response scale

- How should I interpret the effect of each covariate in a GLM?

- In a linear model, this is straightforward, but in a model like our logistic regression for vote choice, the effect of each predictor on the probability scale is non-linear. There's not "an effect"  there are multiple "effects" depending on where I decide to measure.



### Focal Variables

- The [focal]{.yellow} variable is the effect I'm currently interested in measuring. 

- I might be interested in looking at the effect of a simple one unit increase in this variable.

- or I might have something more specific in mind: like measure the effect of going from the minimum value to the maximum, or from -1SD to +1SD. Or I might ask "what would have happened if this specific case had a different value of this variable?"


### Non-Focal Variables

- The [non-focal]{.yellow} variables are any other model coefficients. 

- I'll need to assign values to these to get predictions, but I want to hold them constant so I can isolate the effects of the focal predictors.

- I might want to look at the effect of my focal variable at a specific set of values for the non-focal predictors, or the effect of my focal variable when everything else is at "typical" values.

## Three ways to ask the same question

What is the effect of the Financial Hardship Index (FHI) on the probability of voting for a Republican candidate in the 2026 midterms?
 
- [Marginal Effects for a Specific Case]{.yellow} What is the effect of going from an FHI value of 3 to an FHI value of 4 for a respondent who voted for Trump in 2024?

- [Marginal Effects at Representative Values]{.yellow} What is the effect of increasing FHI by 1 for a respondent with "typical" values of the predictors?
 
- [Average Marginal Effects]{.yellow} What would be the average change if every respondent increased FHI by 1?


### Marginal Effects for a Specific Case

::::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="50%"}
- Run the model
- Create a new data frame containing your hypothetical cases
- Use `predict` with `type='response'` and the `newdata` argument to get predictions for those scenarios on the probability scale.
- Calculate the change in probability when changing the focal predictor.
:::
::: {.column width="50%"}
```{r}
#| echo: true
model<-glm(
  REPVOTE  ~ HARDSHIP_INDEX + VOTE24_CHOICE ,
  family = binomial,
  data = chep)



df <- data.frame(
  HARDSHIP_INDEX = c("HARDSHIP_INDEX" = 3, "HARDSHIP_INDEX" = 4),
  VOTE24_CHOICE = c("(2) Donald Trump", "(2) Donald Trump")
)

df$preds<-predict(model, newdata=df, type='response')

df

```

```{r}
#| echo: true
# the difference in effects
df$preds[2]  - df$preds[1]

```

:::
:::::



### Marginal Effects at Representative Values

::::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="50%"}
- Run the model
- Create a new data frame with typical values for each covariate (for instance, you could use the mode for categorical variables, and the mean or the median for continuous variables)
- Compare
:::
::: {.column width="50%"}
```{r}
#| echo: true
model<-glm(
  REPVOTE  ~ HARDSHIP_INDEX + VOTE24_CHOICE ,
  family = binomial,
  data = chep)



df <- data.frame(
  HARDSHIP_INDEX = c(median(chep$HARDSHIP_INDEX), median(chep$HARDSHIP_INDEX) +1),
  VOTE24_CHOICE = c("(1) Kamala Harris", "(1) Kamala Harris")
)

df$preds<-predict(model, newdata=df, type='response')

df

```

```{r}
#| echo: true
# the difference in effects
df$preds[2]  - df$preds[1]

```

:::
:::::

### Marginal Effects at Representative Values

::::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="50%"}
- You don't necessarily have to look at an increase of +1, you could do something like look at the change from the 25th percentile to the 75th
:::
::: {.column width="50%"}
```{r}
#| echo: true
model<-glm(
  REPVOTE  ~ HARDSHIP_INDEX + VOTE24_CHOICE ,
  family = binomial,
  data = chep)



df <- data.frame(
  HARDSHIP_INDEX = c(1, 6),
  VOTE24_CHOICE = c("(1) Kamala Harris", "(1) Kamala Harris")
)

df$preds<-predict(model, newdata=df, type='response')

df

```

```{r}
#| echo: true
# the difference in effects
df$preds[2]  - df$preds[1]

```

:::
:::::

### Average Marginal Effects

::::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="50%"}
- Get the predicted probability for everyone at their observed values.
- Then, get the predicted probability for everyone after increasing the value of the focal predictor by 1.
- Compare the average difference between the two cases.
:::
::: {.column width="50%"}
```{r}
#| echo: true
model<-glm(
  REPVOTE  ~ HARDSHIP_INDEX + VOTE24_CHOICE ,
  family = binomial,
  data = chep)

df1<-model$data # get the data from the model


df1$preds<-predict(model, newdata=df1, type='response')


df2<-model$data|> # get the data from the model and change the focal predictor
  mutate(HARDSHIP_INDEX = HARDSHIP_INDEX +1 )
df2$preds<-predict(model, newdata=df2, type='response')


# calculate the average differences across all cases
mean(df2$preds - df1$preds, na.rm=T)



```

```{r}
#| echo: true
# the difference in effects
df$preds[2]  - df$preds[1]

```
:::
:::::

### Average Contrasts


::::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="50%"}
- If the focal variable is categorical we would set the focal variable to one category and then change it to another category, while leaving all other responses at their observed values.
:::
::: {.column width="50%"}
```{r}
#| echo: true
model<-glm(
  REPVOTE  ~ HARDSHIP_INDEX + VOTE24_CHOICE ,
  family = binomial,
  data = chep)

df1<-model$data|>
  mutate(VOTE24_CHOICE = "(2) Donald Trump")
  # get the data from the model


df1$preds<-predict(model, newdata=df1, type='response')


df2<-model$data|> # get the data from the model and change the focal predictor
  mutate(VOTE24_CHOICE = "(1) Kamala Harris")
df2$preds<-predict(model, newdata=df2, type='response')


# calculate the average differences across all cases
mean(df2$preds - df1$preds, na.rm=T)



```


:::
:::::


## Some pros and cons

- Average marginal effects are a good default. The main difficulty just the computational burden of making a prediction for every observation in the data set.

- Marginal effects for specific cases can also be a good way to communicate the intuition behind a model, but just note that you should probably pick scenarios with some reason behind them.

## Confidence Intervals

::::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="50%"}
- Getting correct confidence intervals for a non-linear transformation require some extra work as well.

- One reliable (if slow) method is the bootstrap.
:::
::: {.column width="50%"}
```{r}
#| eval: false

# the initial model
model <- glm(REPVOTE  ~ HARDSHIP_INDEX + VOTE24_CHOICE ,
             family = binomial,
             data = chep)

# the number of iterations
nboot<-300
# an empty vector to hold results
mfx<-numeric(nboot)
for(i in 1:nboot) {
  # resampling with replacement from the original data
  boot_data<-model$data[sample(nrow(model$data), replace=T),]
  
  # fitting the model to the bootstrap replicate
  model <- glm(formula(model),
               family = binomial,
               data = boot_data)
  df1 <- model$data |>
    mutate(VOTE24_CHOICE = "(2) Donald Trump")
  # get the data from the model
  df1$preds <- predict(model, newdata = df1, type = 'response')
  df2 <- model$data |> # get the data from the model and change the focal predictor
    mutate(VOTE24_CHOICE = "(1) Kamala Harris")
  df2$preds <- predict(model, newdata = df2, type = 'response')
  # calculate the average differences across all cases
  mfx[i]<-mean(df2$preds - df1$preds, na.rm = T)
  
}

hist(mfx)
quantile(mfx, c(0.025, 0.975))


```

:::
:::::


## Model fit

How well does our model fit the data?

### Model fit

::: incremental
-   In linear regression, we can assess model fit by looking at the distance between the regression line and actual data points.

-   There's not really an analog in logistic regression: we're predicting probabilities, but we only ever see a single outcome for each case. So how do we say anything about the quality of a model?
:::

### Model fit


. . .

The likelihood function:

$$
\begin{align}
\prod^n_{i=1} p_i^{y_i} \times (1-p_i)^{1-y_i}\\
y_i = \text{the actual outcome for an observation}\\
p_i = \text{the predicted outcome for an observation}\\
\prod = \text{the product operator (all these values are multiplied together)}
\end{align}
$$

### Model fit

$$
\begin{align}
\prod^n_{i=1} p_i^{y_i} \times (1-p_i)^{1-y_i}\\
y_i = \text{the actual outcome for an observation}\\
p_i = \text{the predicted outcome for an observation}\\
\prod = \text{the product operator (all these values are multiplied together)}
\end{align}
$$

. . .

If $y_i = 1$ then this simplifies to $p \times 1$

. . .

If $y_i = 0$ then this simplifies to $1-p$

. . .

### Model fit

One method for assessing fit is to compare the likelihood under the fitted model to a "null" model with no predictors.

```{r}
#| echo: true

# the null model
model0<-  glm(REPVOTE  ~ 1 ,
             family = binomial,
             data = chep)
# the comparison
model <- glm(REPVOTE  ~ HARDSHIP_INDEX + VOTE24_CHOICE ,
             family = binomial,
             data = chep)

logLik(model0)
logLik(model1)

```
### Model fit

There are several rough analogs for R^2 based on this comparison. For example, McFadden's $R^2$ value:

$$
\text{McFadden } R^2 = \frac{\text{Null Model LL} - \text{Full Model LL}}{\text{Null Model LL}}
$$

Higher values indicate a greater improvement over the null model:

```{r}

(logLik(model0)- logLik(model1))/logLik(model0)

```

### Model Fit and Model Comparison

- How do we know whether one model is better than any other?

- We could compare log likelihoods, but a more intuitive method might be to see how they each perform on "new" data


#### Leave one out cross-validation

::::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="50%"}
- Drop observation i and fit the model on the remaining data
- Predict the fitted model on observation i
- Repeat for each row in the data
- Compare the accuracy of each result
:::
::: {.column width="50%"}
```{r}
#| echo: true
#| cache: true
predictions<-matrix(nrow=nrow(chep), 
                    ncol=3
                    )

for (i in 1:nrow(chep)) {
  train<-chep[-i,]
  test<-chep[i,]
  model1 <- glm(REPVOTE  ~ VOTE24_CHOICE , 
                family = binomial, 
                data = train)
  
  model2 <- glm(REPVOTE  ~ HARDSHIP_INDEX , 
                family = binomial, 
                data = train)
  
  model3 <- glm(REPVOTE  ~ HARDSHIP_INDEX + VOTE24_CHOICE , 
                family = binomial, 
                data = train)
  
  predictions[i,1]<-predict(model1, newdata=test, type='response')
  predictions[i,2]<-predict(model2, newdata=test, type='response')
  predictions[i,3]<-predict(model3, newdata=test, type='response')
  
  
  
}

table(predictions[,1]>.5, 
      chep$REPVOTE)

table(predictions[,2]>.5, 
      chep$REPVOTE)

table(predictions[,3]>.5, 
      chep$REPVOTE)


```
:::
:::::




#### BIC and AIC

-   BIC stands for Bayesian Information Criteria.
-   AIC stands for Aikake Information Criteria.
-   Both values are based on the model likelihood, which, for linear models, is based on the sum of squared residuals:

. . .

$${\text{BIC} =k \log{(n)}- 2 \log{(L)}}$$

$${\text{AIC} =2k - 2\log{(L)}}$$

Note that both the AIC and BIC include a penalty for `k`, which is the number of model parameters. So both will penalize models with garbage predictors.

## BIC and AIC

Lower values of both AIC and BIC indicate better model fits, but they're only meaningful for comparing between models fitted to the same data.

```{r, echo=TRUE}
  model1 <- glm(REPVOTE  ~ VOTE24_CHOICE , 
                family = binomial, 
                data = train)
  
  model2 <- glm(REPVOTE  ~ HARDSHIP_INDEX , 
                family = binomial, 
                data = chep)
  
  model3 <- glm(REPVOTE  ~ HARDSHIP_INDEX + VOTE24_CHOICE , 
                family = binomial, 
                data = chep)
BIC(model1)
BIC(model2)
BIC(model3)


AIC(model1)
AIC(model2)
AIC(model3)

```

::: notes
in general: lower BIC and AIC scores are better, and an improvement of 10 or more suggests clear improvement. The second part of the expression is a sort of hypothetical maximum for the log likelihood of the entire dataset.
:::
